docs.D01_business_overview.md:
Title: Enterprise distribution, recurring software and Azure
Source: compiled from: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/fy-2026-q2/press-release-webcast; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/events/fy-2026/earnings-fy-2026-q2; https://www.microsoft.com/investor/reports/ar25/index.html
Date: 2026-01-28

Microsoft sells enterprise productivity, cloud infrastructure, business applications, security, operating systems and consumer/gaming products. It reports three segments. Productivity and Business Processes includes Microsoft 365, LinkedIn and Dynamics. Intelligent Cloud includes Azure and server products. More Personal Computing contains Windows, devices, Xbox and search/news advertising. This mix matters: it is neither a pure AI laboratory nor a pure public-cloud supplier.

| Fiscal Q2 2026, dollars millions | Revenue | Operating income |
|---|---:|---:|
| Productivity and Business Processes | 34,116 | 20,599 |
| Intelligent Cloud | 32,907 | 13,873 |
| More Personal Computing | 14,250 | 3,803 calculated residual |
| Total | 81,273 | 38,275 |

The first segment's margin is approximately 60%, Intelligent Cloud's 42%, per the January 28 call. Consolidated operating margin is 47.1%, calculated. More Personal Computing's operating income above is explicitly derived from consolidated income less the first two segments.

The recurring-software moat hypothesis rests on workflows, documents, identity, security and enterprise administration being integrated rather than purchased as independent utilities. Replacing one application is different from replacing an organization's collaboration, permissions, compliance and deployment infrastructure. These are analytical mechanisms suggested by the product architecture, not a guarantee against AI substitution.

Azure benefits from customers moving workloads into managed infrastructure and from AI training/inference demand. However, serving incremental cloud demand requires real capital. Microsoft says customer demand exceeds supply, and allocates some scarce compute internally to Copilot and research. That creates a trade-off between immediately visible Azure revenue and developing other franchises.

Commercial remaining performance obligations reached $625 billion, up 110%. Approximately 45% came from OpenAI. Backlog is not current revenue, cash on hand or riskless earnings; concentration and the time needed to deliver service both matter. Microsoft 365 Copilot had 15 million paid seats and GitHub Copilot more than 4.7 million paid subscribers, per the call.

Satya Nadella is chairman and CEO and Amy Hood CFO. December 31 common shares outstanding were 7,429 million; Q2 diluted weighted-average shares were 7,460 million. The annual report's segment comparison must be used with care because August 2024 reporting changes moved commercial Microsoft 365 activities into Productivity and Business Processes. Current segment growth should not be spliced onto older unrecast definitions.
docs.D02_financial_snapshot.md:
Title: Fiscal-year financial base and investment acceleration
Source: compiled from: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/FY-2025-Q4/income-statements; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/FY-2025-Q4/cash-flows; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/fy-2026-q2/press-release-webcast
Date: 2026-01-28

Microsoft's fiscal year ends June 30. Annual figures were public with the July 2025 fiscal-year release; December-quarter results were released January 28. Dollar amounts below are millions except EPS. Calculated FCF is operating cash flow less cash property/equipment additions; it does not deduct newly incurred finance-lease commitments.

| Metric | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Q2 FY2026 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue | 211,915 | 245,122 | 281,724 | 81,273 |
| Growth | — | 15.7% calculated | 14.9% calculated | 17% |
| Operating income | 88,523 | 109,433 | 128,528 | 38,275 |
| Operating margin, calculated | 41.8% | 44.6% | 45.6% | 47.1% |
| Diluted GAAP EPS | 9.68 | 11.80 | 13.64 | 5.16 |
| Operating cash flow | 87,582 | 118,548 | 136,162 | 35,758 |
| Cash property/equipment additions | 28,107 | 44,477 | 64,551 | 29,876 |
| FCF, calculated | 59,475 | 74,071 | 71,611 | 5,882 |
| Cash dividends paid | 19,800 | 21,771 | 24,082 | 6,762 |
| Cash-flow statement common repurchases | 22,245 | 17,254 | 18,420 | 7,415 |

The cash-flow repurchase row can include equity-award settlement effects and should not be equated automatically to the company's discretionary repurchase-program figure. The earnings headline says $12.7 billion returned through dividends and repurchases in Q2; that differs from mechanically adding the two cash-flow rows. Definitions must remain consistent.

December 31 cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments were $89,462 million. Current long-term debt was $4,837 million and long-term debt $35,425 million. Calculated net cash excluding leases was therefore $49,200 million. This excludes operating leases, finance leases and other commitments. The balance sheet does not look like a debt-refinancing crisis, but that does not remove investment-return risk.

For the six months, CFO was $80,815 million and cash property additions $49,270 million, producing $31,545 million simple FCF. Q2's lower cash conversion is material even alongside a strong first half. Management reports $37.5 billion capex including finance leases for the quarter; that is a different investment measure from cash property additions.

GAAP Q2 EPS includes $1.02 from OpenAI investment gains. Company non-GAAP EPS excluding OpenAI impacts is $4.14, up 24%. Using the $5.16 headline to extrapolate recurring operating growth would overstate the quarter's underlying earnings progression. A consistent historical ROIC measure is not supplied here.
docs.D03_latest_results_and_guidance.md:
Title: January 28 results — growth, allocation constraints and spending
Source: compiled from: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/fy-2026-q2/press-release-webcast; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/events/fy-2026/earnings-fy-2026-q2
Date: 2026-01-28

December-quarter revenue rose 17% to $81.3 billion and operating income 21% to $38.3 billion. Microsoft Cloud revenue crossed $50 billion for the first time, reaching $51.5 billion, up 26%. Azure and other cloud services grew 39% reported, 38% constant currency. Productivity and Business Processes rose 16%, Intelligent Cloud 29%, while More Personal Computing fell 3%.

The GAAP/non-GAAP distinction is unusually important. Net income of $38.458 billion includes OpenAI investment gains; adjusted net income was $30.875 billion. GAAP diluted EPS rose 60% to $5.16, but EPS excluding OpenAI investment impacts rose 24% to $4.14. The comparable prior-year adjustment also removes an OpenAI loss. Neither adjustment is a direct measure of Azure's standalone profitability.

| January 28 outlook/commentary | Public statement |
|---|---|
| Next-quarter Azure growth | 37–38% in constant currency |
| Intelligent Cloud revenue | $34.1–34.4 billion |
| Productivity/Business Processes revenue | $34.25–34.55 billion |
| Next-quarter capex | Expected to decrease sequentially |
| FY2026 operating margins | Expected up slightly |

Quarterly capex was $37.5 billion, with about two-thirds on relatively short-lived GPUs/CPUs and the rest on longer-lived assets. Finance leases were $6.7 billion. Hardware is capitalized and depreciated over six years, per the call. A large current outlay can therefore create later depreciation even if the immediate operating margin appears healthy.

Amy Hood says, “Our customer demand continues to exceed our supply.” She characterizes Azure's outlook as an allocated-capacity guide. Management says using newly available GPUs exclusively for Azure could have put growth above 40%, but it has chosen to support other internal products. That is an allocation explanation, not proof that all those uses generate equal returns.

Hood also says: “The majority of the capital that we’re spending today, and a lot of the GPUs that we’re buying are already contracted for most of their useful life.” Contracted demand supports visibility, while counterparty risk, service costs and realization timing remain relevant.

Nadella explains the goal is not to maximize one business but to allocate capacity to the best lifetime-value portfolio. Investors must distinguish that long-run strategy from a promise to beat every near-term Azure growth expectation. A complete verified calendar-year capital budget and any unannounced future partnership terms remain unavailable for this January review.
docs.D04_price_and_valuation.md:
Title: January 30 closing price, liquidity and earnings normalization
Source: compiled from: https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/MSFT/history/?period1=1769644800&period2=1770163200; https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/29/microsoft-market-cap-earnings.html; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/fy-2026-q2/press-release-webcast; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/FY-2025-Q4/income-statements; https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/msft?__source=newsletter%7Cwarrenbuffettwatch
Date: 2026-01-30

January 30's historical unadjusted close was $430.29, with open $439.17, high $439.60, low $426.45 and volume 58,566,800. January 29 closed at $433.50 on 128,855,300 shares. CNBC's January 29 report describes a roughly 10% one-day fall, $357 billion market-cap loss and $3.22 trillion remaining capitalization.

A CNBC quote observation dated October 2025 gives a $555.45 high reached July 31, 2025 and $344.79 low reached April 7, 2025. These are pre-cutoff observations, not an independently refreshed January 30 rolling range. The January 30 price is 22.5% below that already-observed high, calculated. It is 0.74% below January 29's close.

Multiplying the January 30 close by 7.429 billion December 31 common shares yields a calculated equity-value proxy of $3.197 trillion. Using $49.2 billion net cash excluding leases yields a corresponding EV proxy of $3.147 trillion. These calculations use a month-old share count and exclude lease obligations; they are not exact market-vendor observations.

FY2025 EPS $13.64 less prior first-half FY2025 EPS $6.53 plus first-half FY2026 EPS $8.87 gives approximately $15.98 trailing GAAP EPS. This sum-of-period bridge is approximate because diluted share denominators differ. The resulting calculated trailing P/E is 26.9x. Current half-year OpenAI gains and prior-year OpenAI losses make that multiple an imperfect representation of recurring operations. The pack does not supply every quarterly adjustment needed for an exact normalized trailing series.

Trailing CFO can be bridged as $136.162bn−$56.471bn+$80.815bn=$160.506bn. Cash property additions similarly total $83.094bn, leaving simple trailing FCF of $77.412bn. Against the equity-value proxy, that is a calculated 2.4% FCF yield before finance-lease adjustments.

A date-authenticated January 30 forward EPS consensus, forward P/E, EV/EBITDA, S&P 500 forward P/E and full five-to-ten-year Microsoft multiple range were not recovered. Any estimate requires a dated earnings denominator and consistent accounting treatment. The available evidence supports a substantial drawdown and a calculable trailing valuation, but not a falsely precise forward entry multiple. Building a billion-dollar position appears feasible relative to the observed daily volume, subject to participation limits and execution costs.
docs.D05_market_worries.md:
Title: Sell-side debate — Azure execution and whether Copilot earns its compute
Source: compiled from: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/29/microsoft-market-cap-earnings.html; https://www.morningstar.com/stocks/microsoft-earnings-good-quarter-with-ai-demand-ramping-azure-good; https://fortune.com/2026/01/28/microsoft-stock-drops-azure-growth-slows-capex-spending-q2/
Date: 2026-01-29

Jordan Novet's January 29 CNBC report gives a precise explanation for the negative reaction. Azure grew 39%, below StreetAccount's 39.4% consensus. The next-quarter More Personal Computing revenue outlook of about $12.6 billion was below $13.7 billion consensus, and implied operating margin also disappointed. Thus the selloff was not caused by reported revenue declining across the whole company.

The more important strategic question is capital allocation. CNBC reports that Microsoft prioritized internal AI applications over allocating all new compute to external Azure customers. UBS analysts led by Karl Keirstead wrote: “M365 revs growth is not accelerating due to Copilot” and said many customer checks did not show a strong usage ramp. They concluded: “We think Microsoft needs to 'prove' that these are good investments.” These are dated analyst observations, not established product-failure facts.

Melius Research's Ben Reitzes, still with a buy rating, offered a different criticism: “there's an execution issue here with Azure, where they need to literally stand up buildings a little faster.” This argues for more effective capacity delivery, not less demand. The two criticisms can coexist: poor allocation or slow construction can prevent strong customer demand from becoming attractive shareholder returns.

Bernstein analysts led by Mark Moerdler defended management's conscious decision to focus on the company's long-term interests rather than maximizing the current quarter's share price. Morningstar's Dan Romanoff, January 29, maintained a $600 fair-value estimate and highlighted broad cloud demand. He noted RPO rose 110%, but 28% excluding OpenAI. The comparison is important because backlog concentration can make an aggregate growth figure look stronger than the diversified customer base.

Fortune's January 28 account, published around the earnings release, juxtaposes slower Azure growth with elevated spending and continuing capacity constraints. The underlying bear mechanism is that revenue growth, current margins and the service lives of expensive equipment may not support adequate returns on the expanded capital base.

Additional analytical risks include AI reducing software seats, alternative models capturing value instead of the platform, and OpenAI financing obligations becoming harder to fulfill. None is a demonstrated outcome at the cutoff. Conversely, paid Copilot seats and growing cloud demand do not alone prove successful incremental monetization. The decision requires separating a durable distribution franchise from potentially lower-return new investment.
docs.D06_peers_and_industry.md:
Title: Platform economics compared with other hyperscalers
Source: compiled from: https://s206.q4cdn.com/479360582/files/doc_news/2025/Oct/29/attachments/2025q3-alphabet-earnings-release.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000101872425000121/amzn-20250930xex991.htm; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/fy-2026-q2/press-release-webcast; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/events/fy-2026/earnings-fy-2026-q2
Date: 2026-01-28

Microsoft competes with Amazon and Alphabet in cloud services, with a broader set of vendors in productivity, security and AI. These businesses have overlapping infrastructure needs but different monetization routes. Microsoft's installed enterprise relationships connect cloud, productivity, identity and administration; Amazon's mix includes low-margin retail; Alphabet's includes search and video advertising. Consolidated P/E and margins are not standalone cloud comparisons.

The explicitly dated benchmark figures below come from Q3 2025 peer releases and Microsoft's December-quarter release. They are not synchronized calendar quarters or a claim that October releases remain every peer's latest available report.

| Business/period | Revenue | Reported growth | Relevant profitability observation |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Microsoft, December quarter | $81.273bn | 17% | 47.1% calculated operating margin |
| Intelligent Cloud, December quarter | $32.907bn | 29% | Approximately 42% operating margin |
| Azure/other cloud, December quarter | Not separately disclosed | 39%, 38% constant currency | Standalone operating income not disclosed |
| Amazon, September quarter | $180.2bn | 13% | $17.4bn operating income including special charges |
| AWS, September quarter | $33.0bn | 20% | Do not infer Azure margin from AWS |
| Alphabet, September quarter | $102.346bn | 16% | 31% operating margin including EC fine |

Microsoft's Productivity and Business Processes margin of about 60% is evidence that the existing enterprise-software base has economics different from infrastructure rental. That base may fund the investment cycle and distribute new AI capabilities. However, a profitable installed base can also subsidize lower-return experiments; the source of cash does not determine the return on its use.

Compute availability, energy, networking and construction execution constrain hyperscaler supply. The January call says Microsoft is allocating capacity among Azure, its own applications and research. A peer's faster revenue growth may reflect different available capacity, business mix or starting size rather than superior underlying demand.

Contemporaneous cutoff forward multiples and harmonized FCF yields for the peers were not authenticated. No later market-data row is backfilled. The available comparison is operating growth and economic structure, not a complete relative-value ranking. A careful analyst should avoid using Microsoft's much higher consolidated margin as proof its cloud business is inherently superior to AWS or Google Cloud, or using a lower peer P/E without adjusting for cash, nonoperating gains and business mix.
docs.D07_event_timeline.md:
Title: From OpenAI restructuring to the January earnings reset
Source: compiled from: https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2025/10/28/the-next-chapter-of-the-microsoft-openai-partnership/; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/earnings/fy-2026-q2/press-release-webcast; https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/29/microsoft-market-cap-earnings.html; https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/MSFT/history/?period1=1769644800&period2=1770163200
Date: 2026-01-30

October 28, 2025: Microsoft and OpenAI announced a revised partnership following OpenAI's recapitalization. Microsoft's investment in OpenAI Group PBC was valued at about $135 billion, representing approximately 27% on an as-converted diluted basis. This is an equity holding, not cash in Microsoft's bank account and not annual operating profit. The same announcement said OpenAI contracted to buy an incremental $250 billion in Azure services.

The agreement preserves important IP and cloud rights while changing their boundaries. Microsoft retains model and product IP rights through 2032, including post-AGI models. Confidential research-method rights continue until verified AGI or 2030, whichever is earlier. An independent expert panel must verify an OpenAI declaration of AGI. Consumer hardware is excluded from Microsoft's IP rights.

Azure API exclusivity remains until AGI, but OpenAI can serve non-API products on other clouds and Microsoft no longer holds a right of first refusal to supply compute. Certain US national-security API uses can operate regardless of cloud provider. Microsoft may independently pursue AGI, including with third parties. These nuances argue against treating the partnership as either perpetual total exclusivity or a complete separation.

January 28, 2026: The December-quarter release reported $81.3 billion revenue, 39% reported Azure growth and $625 billion commercial RPO. The earnings call disclosed that about 45% of that RPO was OpenAI-related. The equity stake, recognized investment gains and service commitments are different exposures to the same partner; they should not be counted as three independent sources of diversification.

January 29: Shares fell about 10%; CNBC reported a $357 billion capitalization loss. Debate centered on Azure missing a narrow consensus expectation, capacity allocation, Copilot monetization and the $37.5 billion quarterly capital program.

January 30: Historical unadjusted close was $430.29, following the prior session's $433.50. This is the first trading day after the main earnings-related selloff, and the cutoff used here. Outcomes of the next results, subsequent partnership changes and future AI spending announcements are unknown.

There is no verified CEO replacement or activist campaign in this timeline. The public route to demonstrating value is operating execution: converting contracted demand into revenue, validating paid AI usage, controlling costs and earning acceptable returns on infrastructure. The dates establish what can be known, not which of those outcomes will occur.
docs.D08_pershing_context.md:
Title: Public portfolio context at January 30
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/15162701/PSH-Fact-Sheet-December-2025-Website.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/20192925/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-June-2025-Interim.pdf; https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/facing-losses-ackman-exits-chipotle-and-nike; https://finance.yahoo.com/news/bill-ackman-bets-2-magnificent-212245570.html
Date: 2026-01-15

The December 31 PSH fact sheet was published January 15. It reports $15.536 billion equity before accrued performance-fee deductions and $19.187 billion gross AUM including debt principal. Debt-to-total-capital was 19.5%. Neither number is the manager's total firm AUM; nor does gross AUM represent cash available for a new purchase.

Publicly disclosed holdings listed are Alphabet, Amazon, Brookfield, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Hertz, Hilton, Howard Hughes, Pershing Square SPARC, Restaurant Brands, Seaport, Uber and Universal Music. The fact sheet explicitly updates the holdings list only after an investment is disclosed, and removes a position only after an exit is disclosed. It is therefore a public-information set, not a guarantee of complete current economic exposure.

The latest US 13F available by January 30 is the September-quarter filing made November 14; the December-quarter filing is not yet public. Complete independently authenticated line-item weights from that filing are not included here. An older June-quarter secondary report gave rough reported-book weights of 21% Uber, 19% Brookfield, 11% Restaurant Brands and 9.3% Amazon. Those are stale perimeter-specific observations, not January NAV weights. Exact January cash is unavailable. H1 reported $1.404 billion June 30 cash against $14.715 billion net assets.

Public November 21 Institutional Investor coverage of the November investor call says Chipotle and Nike exposure was exited, with Nike's remaining exposure in options. This predates the cutoff. The story incorrectly says the original Chipotle purchase was in 2015; that incidental date is not relied upon. Canadian Pacific's April exit was already disclosed in the August H1 report.

The fact sheet states that the substantial majority of the portfolio is normally allocated to 8–12 core positions, typically liquid listed North American large caps. It emphasizes “high-quality growth businesses” with limited downside and “predictable, recurring cash flows.” It describes normally only one to three new core investments per year and selective governance/operating intervention, with opportunistic hedging.

Existing Alphabet and Amazon exposures make additional enterprise-platform exposure relevant to concentration and correlated AI capital-spending risk. No authenticated Microsoft-specific pre-cutoff Ackman thesis quotation is available in these materials. Later letters or filings cannot be used to fill the January information gap. This context supplies capital-allocation constraints, not a recommendation about Microsoft.

drivers.driver: M365 is an embedded enterprise workflow platform rather than an easily displaced point solution.
drivers.quote: Unlike point software solutions, which may be vulnerable to disintermediation by better-performing AI alternatives, M365 is tightly integrated into the daily workflow of nearly every large enterprise

drivers.driver: Azure benefits from secular migration and AI demand, with multiple-model distribution.
Copilot and consumption-based monetization can expand the valuable existing enterprise bundle.
The post-results decline offered an attractive multiple with additional OpenAI equity value.
drivers.quote: We were able to establish our position at a valuation of 21 times forward earnings

answer_key.pack_quality_notes: 8 documents. Changed cutoff to January 30, first trading day after January 29 ~10% drop, before February purchases. January 30 $430.29 historical close authenticated. Forward multiple, own-history range, cutoff peer multiples and exact current cash/portfolio weights unavailable; not filled with later manager numbers. Three-year financials primary-source verified. Drivers with null quote are paraphrases, not invented verbatim text. No February/May spending budgets or April OpenAI amendments in pack.

valuation.downside_case: Valuation contraction to 18-20x P/E if AI capex fails to generate commensurate returns.

drivers.driver: The company maintains a dominant position in essential enterprise software and cloud infrastructure with high margins and a fortress balance sheet.
A 22.5% drawdown from July 2025 highs provides an attractive entry point for a high-quality compounder growing cloud revenue at 39%.
Satya Nadella has demonstrated exceptional stewardship, prioritizing long-term lifetime value over short-term quarterly results.
Market concerns regarding AI infrastructure spending and OpenAI financing are temporary dislocations that ignore the long-term monetization potential of Copilot.

kill_criteria: Sustained deceleration in cloud revenue growth below 20% for two consecutive quarters.
Copilot and AI-integrated product adoption fails to translate into margin expansion or FCF growth within 18 months.
Management shifts to aggressive, low-return acquisitions to mask organic growth stagnation.
Infrastructure bottlenecks lead to chronic loss of market share to AWS or Google Cloud.
final.what_would_change_our_mind: Evidence that AI-related capital expenditure has become a permanent structural drag on margins rather than a growth-enabling investment.
final.memo:
Microsoft represents a classic Pershing Square quality compounder: a dominant, free-cash-flow-generative business with deep moats in enterprise software and identity infrastructure [D01]. With a net cash position of $49.200bn and sustained double-digit revenue growth, the company meets our highest standards for simplicity, predictability, and financial strength [D01], [D02].

The current market dislocation, marked by a 22.5% drawdown from the July 2025 peak, is driven by an overreaction to elevated capital expenditures and OpenAI financing commitments [D04], [D05]. We believe these outlays are essential to secure long-term leadership in cloud and enterprise AI, rather than a permanent impairment of intrinsic value [D01], [D03].

At a 26.9x trailing P/E, we are acquiring a dominant franchise at an attractive valuation [D04]. With cloud growth at 39% and a consolidated operating margin of ~47%, we expect a 15% EPS CAGR over the next several years as AI-integrated products like Copilot move from development to scale [D01], [D03].

Our role is that of a long-term owner relying on the compounding of intrinsic value [D01]. We expect a natural re-rating as the market shifts its focus from infrastructure spending cycles to the tangible monetization of cloud-based AI [D03]. We have sized this at 8% of NAV, mindful of our existing exposure to hyperscalers, to provide meaningful upside while managing aggregate concentration risk [D05], [D08].

valuation.eps_path: 15% CAGR based on sustained cloud and AI scaling
valuation.downside_case: Multiple compression to 20x if AI monetization fails

drivers.driver: Microsoft is a dominant, mission-critical enterprise franchise with high pricing power and a fortress balance sheet holding $49.2 billion in net cash [D01], [D02].
The market has incorrectly punished the stock following earnings due to short-term capex concerns, ignoring that 39% Azure growth validates the long-term AI strategy [D03], [D04].
Satya Nadella continues to demonstrate superior capital allocation by prioritizing the lifetime value of the ecosystem over short-term capacity constraints [D03].
The company’s ability to drive double-digit revenue growth through cloud and AI integration provides a reliable path to mid-teens EPS expansion [D02], [D03].

kill_criteria: Azure revenue growth decelerates below 25% for two consecutive quarters.
Management shifts capital allocation away from core high-margin software/cloud infrastructure.
Evidence of meaningful enterprise customer churn from the Microsoft ecosystem.
Free cash flow conversion remains structurally impaired without a path to margin expansion.
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A fundamental shift where AI infrastructure spending fails to convert into sustainable, high-margin software revenue, permanently impairing the company's long-term FCF conversion and return on capital.
final.memo:
Microsoft represents one of the most durable and free-cash-flow-generative businesses in the global economy [D01]. With a dominant #1 or #2 position in cloud infrastructure and enterprise productivity, the firm possesses significant pricing power and deep competitive moats through its integrated security and identity ecosystem [D01].

Currently, the market is mispricing the company due to excessive focus on near-term capital expenditure and short-term capacity constraints [D04], [D05]. Investors have reflexiveley sold off the stock following earnings, failing to recognize that 39% Azure growth is a powerful indicator of secular demand that outweighs current capex intensity [D03], [D04].

We were able to acquire our initial stake at a 26.9x trailing P/E, a valuation that is compelling for a business of this quality [D04]. Given our expectation for 15% EPS growth and a terminal multiple of 28x, we anticipate an attractive internal rate of return, well-supported by the firm's $49.2 billion net cash position [D02], [D03], [D04].

Our role is that of a long-term compounder, allowing management to execute its AI-native transformation without the pressure of quarterly volatility [D03]. We will monitor Azure growth and the normalization of capital expenditure closely to ensure the core enterprise franchise remains resilient [D03], [D05].

The primary risk to our thesis is that the significant capital expenditure required for AI infrastructure fails to yield sufficient incremental revenue, which would lower the firm's long-term FCF conversion [D02], [D05]. We have mitigated this by focusing on the company's mission-critical nature and fortress balance sheet, which provide a significant margin of safety [D02].

We are initiating a position at 3% of NAV today, with a plan to scale to 6% of NAV as we gain further confidence in the long-term AI-driven margin expansion [D04]. Despite our existing exposure to other cloud providers, we believe Microsoft's unique ecosystem dominance justifies this concentration [D08].
